strengths: The core insight is well-motivated and clearly supported: Fig. 2 quantifies that semantic-mask overlap is highest within supercategories, and Fig. 3 shows instance structure emerges in self-attention before semantics, providing a principled basis for the instance-first, two-phase design rather than an ad hoc heuristic.

The method is genuinely training-free and model-agnostic, and this is backed by an unusually broad empirical validation: nine diffusion backbones (SD1.4/1.5/2.1, SDXL, SD3.5-M/L, PixArt-α/Σ, Flux.1-dev, Qwen-Image), plus layout-to-image (GLIGEN) and fine-tuned models (TokenCompose, IterComp), demonstrating both applicability and complementarity.

Comparison against count-supervised methods (CountGen, Counting Guidance) is a strong and fair test: ISAC surpasses them on counting accuracy without auxiliary networks or fine-tuning, and Tab. 10 shows complementarity, which strengthens rather than weakens the claim.

Ablations are convincing and targeted: the loss-schedule ablation (Tab. 5) directly supports the instance-to-semantic ordering hypothesis, the MPO ablation (Tab. 6) isolates the contribution of the max-overlap formulation, and clustering-algorithm and step-size sensitivity analyses are provided.

The evaluation is thoughtfully constructed: IntraCompBench fills a real gap (intra-class compositions where failures concentrate), uses an ensemble of three detectors with a 2-of-3 agreement rule, seeds are varied (10 per prompt), and stability analysis across 30 seeds is reported. FID/CMMD are included to check the quality–accuracy trade-off.

Efficiency concerns are honestly addressed: latency/VRAM are reported alongside accuracy, a gradient-free latent-selection variant (ISAC_LS) is provided for large models, and layer-wise analysis (Tab. 14) identifies a path to reducing overhead.
The paper acknowledges a concrete limitation (lack of 3D awareness, Fig. 15) rather than presenting only favorable examples.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' framing is somewhat qualified in practice: ISAC depends on an LLM-based parser (GPT-OSS-20B) that takes ~10 s and ~40 GB VRAM per prompt to extract counts, attributes, and token relations. This external dependency, its failure modes, and its overhead should be more prominently acknowledged as part of the method's cost, particularly since parsing errors directly affect instance masks and losses.

ISAC requires explicit instance counts at inference (acknowledged in Tab. 1), which limits applicability to prompts with unambiguous numerals; the authors themselves note ambiguous counts ('a few', 'several') are unresolved. This is a real scope restriction relative to the broad 'model-agnostic, robust multi-object generation' framing.

The headline improvements are heavily concentrated on the self-introduced IntraCompBench. Gains on existing public benchmarks are smaller and less uniform (e.g., T2I-CompBench 'Complex' is nearly unchanged for SD1.5: 0.354 vs 0.353), so the generality of the contribution beyond intra-class/similar-object settings is less demonstrated than the abstract suggests.

Image-quality assessment is thin: FID/CMMD in Tab. 13 are computed only against the native SDXL distribution on a single task, with '0.0000' for the baseline, and no human evaluation or aesthetics study is provided; with a max-based repel objective operating on attention masks, heavier qualitative checks for artifacts across seeds would strengthen the claims.

Several design choices appear empirically rather than analytically grounded and are justified only post hoc via ablations: the linear λ_ins(t) = t/T schedule, the max-over MPO penalty (which could be sensitive to the single worst pixel), and min-max vs softmax CA normalization. The paper would benefit from brief analysis of when/why these choices could fail.

Computational overhead is significant (~2.5× latency, ~2–3.3× VRAM), and the per-step clustering (K-means, ~505 ms/step) plus backpropagation through all attention layers may limit practicality for real-time or very large models despite the ISAC_LS alternative.

Conceptually, the method composes known components (self-attention clustering as in prior instance-discovery work, repel-style contrastive losses as in SynGen/CONFORM, latent optimization as in A&E); the novelty lies mainly in the hierarchical decoupling, the MPO formulation, and the schedule rather than in fundamentally new machinery, which reviewers should weigh when judging originality.

strengths: The core insight — that instance formation (from self-attention) should precede semantic assignment (in cross-attention) — is well motivated and supported by analysis (Fig. 2, Fig. 3), and the two-phase hierarchical objective (L_ins then L_sem) is a clean, principled instantiation of this hypothesis.

The method is training-free and evaluated remarkably broadly: nine diffusion backbones (SD1.4/1.5/2.1, SDXL, SD3.5-M/L, PixArt-α/Σ, Flux.1-dev) across three text-to-image benchmarks, plus layout-to-image (GLIGEN) and fine-tuned model integrations (Tab. 12), and a latent-selection variant for large models (Alg. 2, Tab. 11).

Ablations are substantive: the loss-schedule experiment (Tab. 5) directly tests the instance-first hypothesis (instance-only vs. semantic-only vs. reversed schedule), the MPO vs. MAE/KL/IoU comparison (Tab. 6) isolates the similarity-metric choice, and clustering-algorithm/coordinate-concatenation details (Tab. 7, Fig. 9) justify design decisions.

IntraCompBench addresses a genuine gap: existing benchmarks do not isolate the intra-class regime where count failures and semantic mixing are most severe, and the 2–5-object design with a detector-ensemble protocol is reasonable.
The paper is transparent about limitations (3D/occlusion failure mode, C.5), image-quality trade-off (FID/CMMD in Tab. 13), VRAM overhead, and seed-stability variance reduction.
Table 1 is honest that ISAC requires instance counts at inference, and the paper openly positions itself against count-supervised baselines rather than hiding this dependency.
weaknesses: The 'no extra models / training-free' framing is somewhat undermined in practice: the pipeline depends on GPT-OSS-20B for prompt parsing (a 20B-parameter model needing ~40GB VRAM and 10s per prompt), plus a three-detector ensemble (Grounding DINO, YOLOE, YOLOv12) for benchmark construction. The contribution remains training-free, but 'model-agnostic, requires only attention maps' claims should be softened.

Evaluation-protocol concerns: ISAC uses min-max CA normalization while baselines use softmax normalization (Eq. 12 vs. 13); this means part of the large gains on HRS/T2I-CompBench (e.g., the suspicious doubling of SD1.5 spatial score 0.127→0.263) may stem from this confound rather than the instance-first principle. An ablation isolating the normalization choice is missing.

The benchmark is proposed by the authors and evaluated with their own detector-ensemble and matching rules; accuracy is partial-credit (3/5=60%), which can mask persistent missing objects and may interact favorably with the method's strong at-#2 performance. Independent validation of IntraCompBench on other methods' official numbers would strengthen credibility.

The quality–accuracy trade-off, while disclosed, is non-trivial: FID of 16.4 vs. 0.0 baseline (Tab. 13) indicates a substantial distributional shift, and several qualitative panels (e.g., Fig. 5, 'a yellow person, a red cat, and a blue banana') show noticeably artifact-heavy, unnatural renders. Human evaluation of perceptual quality is absent.

Inference cost roughly doubles to triples (latency and VRAM, Tab. 2), which limits practicality; the layer-selection efficiency study (Tab. 14) is deferred to an appendix and not integrated into the main results.

The dependence on accurate instance counts limits applicability to prompts with explicit numerals (acknowledged for ambiguous counts, but 'a few dogs'-type prompts are common in practice); the HRS-Bench spatial/size gains are hard to explain by the method's stated mechanism and warrant scrutiny.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence: 'first training-free method to achieve instance-level control' relies on a specific reading of prior count-supervised work, and the abstract's 'improvements of at least 50%' is a relative claim on the authors' own benchmark rather than an absolute gain.

strengths: Well-motivated analysis: the paper provides a clear diagnosis (semantic-mask overlap within supercategories and SA/CA mismatch causing count failures and semantic mixing) backed by quantitative evidence (Fig. 2 Dice heatmaps) and temporal dynamics visualization (Fig. 3), which motivates the instance-first design principle rather than just proposing a tweak.

The two-phase hierarchical formulation (Lins for class-agnostic instance formation, Lsem for instance-aware semantic binding) is clean, principled, and the algorithm is training-free and model-agnostic, requiring only one hyperparameter (η).

Very comprehensive empirical evidence: consistent gains across three benchmarks and an unusually wide range of backbones (SD1.4/1.5/2.1, SDXL, SD3.5-M/L, PixArt-α/Σ, Flux, Qwen-Image), including layout-to-image (GLIGEN) and fine-tuned models (TokenCompose, IterComp), plus a latent-selection variant for large models—well beyond typical papers in this area.

Thorough ablations: loss schedule (Tab. 5), MPO vs. alternative metrics (Tab. 6), clustering algorithms (Tab. 7), step-size sensitivity (Fig. 8), seed stability (Tab. 16), image-quality trade-off via FID/CMMD (Tab. 13), and complementarity with CountGen (Tab. 10).

New benchmark (IntraCompBench) targeting the intra-class regime where failures concentrate; the evaluation protocol (2-of-3 detector ensemble, 10 seeds per prompt) is described in enough detail to be reproducible.

Strong ablation support for the core claim: instance-only gets high instance accuracy but low class accuracy, semantic-only the reverse, and the instance-to-semantic schedule dominates both, directly validating the hierarchical hypothesis.
Honest limitations discussion (3D/occlusion failure mode, ambiguous count expressions, VRAM overhead) with constructive future-work directions.
weaknesses: The method requires per-prompt instance counts supplied via an LLM parser (GPT-OSS), which is a form of inference-time supervision comparable to count-supervised baselines; while the comparison to CountGen/Counting Guidance is fair in spirit, the dependence on external LLM parsing (40GB VRAM, ~10s per prompt) somewhat weakens the 'minimal cues' framing and adds a component whose failure modes on complex prompts are only briefly analyzed.

The headline gains come largely from the self-introduced IntraCompBench, evaluated with the authors' own detection-ensemble protocol; improvements on established benchmarks (T2I-CompBench, HRS-Bench) are solid but smaller in relative terms, so the 'at least 50%/1.9x' abstract claims should be read cautiously as being driven by the new benchmark. Independent replication of the benchmark would strengthen it.

Conceptual novelty is moderate: Phase 2's repel/bind losses are acknowledged to follow prior work (SynGen, CONFORM), and SA clustering into instances builds on known observations (Diffegg, InitNO); the contribution is the hierarchical composition and the MPO objective rather than fundamentally new machinery. The strong MPO ablation (Tab. 6) helps, but the delta over prior work is mostly architectural packaging.

Significant inference overhead: 2-3.3x VRAM and ~2-3x latency from backprop through all attention layers; the layer-selection analysis (Tab. 14) shows a promising mitigation (mid-block only, same VRAM, 31.7s vs. 111.4s on SDXL) but accuracy under the reduced variant is not reported, so the practical efficiency story is incomplete.

Some presentation issues: Table 1's column semantics ('Require instance counts at inference phase') can be confusing when read against the text; FID/CMMD in Tab. 13 measure deviation from the native SDXL distribution rather than a reference dataset, which inflates interpretability of 'excellent visual fidelity'; minor typos ('Seperation', 'witth', 'ItraCompBench').

Bounded Attention is excluded from layout comparisons with argued justification, but this means a key competing training-free layout method is not quantitatively compared; a numerical result, even under the authors' adapted protocol, would be more convincing than qualitative failure cases alone.
